questions.prompt: You need a checkout of a branch named `release-2` that already exists, in a folder outside your repository, because `claude --worktree` always starts a new branch from the default. Which command gets you there?
questions.explanation: `git worktree add <path> <branch>` checks out an existing branch into a new folder. Option A is the tempting wrong answer because it is the command from the previous lesson, but `--worktree` creates a new branch (`worktree-<name>`) rather than checking out one that exists. Option B switches your current folder onto the branch and risks carrying uncommitted work, and a clone is a separate repository, not a shared worktree.

questions.prompt: You commit inside `../wt-drill-fix` and then look at `git log` from your main folder. The commit is not on `main` but `git log fix-issue-456` shows it. Why can the main folder see a commit made somewhere else?
options: Both worktrees share the repository's object store and refs, so the commit exists once and is reachable from both
The worktree copied the commit back to the main folder on exit
Git stores worktree commits in a temporary area until you merge
The commit is only visible because the worktree is still on disk
questions.explanation: A worktree shares the repository's `.git`; a commit is written once and its branch label is a ref in that shared repo, so the main checkout can read it immediately. Option D is the tempting wrong answer because it sounds plausible — but the commit survives `git worktree remove`, which is exactly the point of Build It step 5. Nothing is copied back, and there is no staging area for cross-worktree commits.

questions.prompt: You run `git switch fix-issue-456` in your main folder while a worktree already has that branch checked out. Git refuses. What is the refusal protecting you from?
options: Losing commits that are only reachable from the worktree
A merge that would create a conflict between the two folders
Two folders editing and committing to the same branch at the same time
questions.explanation: Git enforces one worktree per branch so two folders cannot move the same label out from under each other. Option B is the tempting wrong answer because 'two checkouts' sounds like a merge, but no merge happens — the hazard is concurrent writes to one branch, not divergent histories. Losing unreachable commits is what the reflog covers, not this rule.

questions.prompt: A colleague made a worktree by hand with `git worktree add`, edited two files, and never committed. Their session ends. What reclaims that folder, and what happens to the edits?
options: Claude Code's cleanup sweep removes it and the edits are lost
Nothing automatic removes it; the edits stay in the folder until they remove it, and then the edits are gone
The edits are pushed to the remote automatically on exit
Git commits the edits to the branch so they are safe
questions.explanation: Claude Code's sweep only manages worktrees it created — a manual worktree is the user's to remove, so nothing reclaims it automatically. The uncommitted edits live only in that folder and vanish when it is removed. Option A is the tempting wrong answer for anyone who read that the sweep 'keeps worktrees with work'; that rule applies to worktrees Claude Code created, not the one added by hand. Nothing auto-pushes or auto-commits.
